questions.q: An int pointer iptr holds address 1000. On a system where an int is 4 bytes, what address does iptr hold after iptr++?
questions.explain: Incrementing a pointer moves it to the next storage location of the type it points to. The next int is 4 bytes away, so the address goes from 1000 to 1004.

questions.q: A char pointer cptr holds address 2000. What address does cptr hold after cptr++?
questions.explain: A char takes 1 byte, so the next valid char address is 1 byte beyond the current one.

questions.q: True or false: For any pointer type, ptr = ptr + N makes ptr point N elements (storage locations of the pointed-to type) beyond where it pointed before.
questions.explain: The meaning of pointer arithmetic is the same for every type: adding N moves the pointer N elements forward, whatever the type.

questions.q: True or false: Incrementing a char pointer increases its numeric address value by 4.
questions.explain: A char is 1 byte, so cptr++ adds 1 to the address. Adding 4 bytes is what happens for an int pointer when int is 4 bytes.

questions.q: A programmer writes ptr++. What decides how many bytes the compiler-generated code actually adds to ptr's value?
choices: The size of the type ptr points to
Always 1 byte, whatever the type
The total size of the array ptr points into
The value stored at the address ptr currently points to
questions.explain: The compiler adds the number of bytes used to store the pointed-to type, so the pointer lands on the next valid address of that type.

questions.q: An int pointer p holds address 500 (int is 4 bytes). What address does p hold after p = p + 3?
questions.explain: p + 3 moves 3 ints forward: 3 * 4 = 12 bytes, so 500 + 12 = 512.

questions.q: Given int numbers[10]; int *iptr;, which expression is equivalent to iptr = numbers;?
choices: iptr = &(numbers[0]);
iptr = numbers[0];
iptr = *numbers;
iptr = &numbers[1];
questions.explain: An array name used this way gives the address of its first element, so numbers is the same as &(numbers[0]).

questions.q: Why should a pointer used to walk through an array have the same type as the array's elements (for example, char * for a char array)?
choices: The pointer's type sets how far each increment moves, so a matching type lands on each element in turn
C does not allow any pointer to be incremented unless it points to an array
Matching types makes the array bigger
Dereferencing a pointer only works if it points to element 0
questions.explain: Each increment moves the pointer by the size of its pointed-to type. If that type matches the element type, every increment moves exactly one element.
On iteration i = 4, cptr points to letters[4] and stores 'a' + 4, which is 'e'.
On iteration i = 7, iptr points to numbers[7] and stores 7 * 3 = 21.

questions.q: True or false: In a loop over i, dereferencing a pointer and then doing ptr++ each iteration visits the same array elements as reading ptr[i] from a pointer that stays at the base of the array.
questions.explain: Incrementing the pointer once per iteration moves it to element i on iteration i. That is the same element ptr[i] reaches when ptr stays at the base.

questions.q: char *cptr starts at address 3000 and int *iptr starts at address 4000 (int is 4 bytes). Each is incremented once per iteration in a 10-iteration loop. What address does iptr hold after the loop?
questions.explain: Each iptr++ adds 4 bytes, so 10 increments add 40: 4000 + 40 = 4040. (cptr would end at 3010.)

questions.q: Compared with array indexing, what is the main drawback of using pointer arithmetic to access array elements?
choices: It is easier to make mistakes, and those mistakes are harder to debug
It cannot change array elements, only read them
It works only on char arrays
It always runs slower than indexing
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic is error-prone and harder to debug than indexing. Indexing is usually the better choice, but stepping a pointer through an array is sometimes convenient.
iptr starts at index 2. Adding 4 moves it 4 int elements forward to index 6.

questions.q: Given int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; int *p = a; p += 3;, what is the value of *p?
questions.explain: p starts at a[0]. Adding 3 moves it to a[3], which holds 40.

choices: numbers[2] is -13
numbers[6] is 9999
numbers[3] is unchanged (9)
numbers[4] is 9999
numbers[0] is -13
questions.explain: Only the elements at index 2 and index 6 change. Every other element keeps its original value.
A statically declared 2D array is stored row by row in contiguous memory, so matrix[3][5] is 3*20 + 5 = 65 elements from the start.

questions.q: After filling int matrix[10][20] with consecutive values 0, 1, 2, ... using a single incrementing int pointer that starts at &matrix[0][0], which element holds the value 45?
choices: matrix[2][5]
matrix[4][5]
matrix[5][4]
matrix[0][45]
questions.explain: Each row has 20 elements. 45 = 2*20 + 5, so the value 45 is in row 2, column 5.

questions.q: Why can one int pointer, set once to &matrix[0][0] and then incremented, visit every element of a statically declared int matrix[N][M]?
choices: All of the array's elements sit in one contiguous block of memory, one row after another
The compiler resets the pointer to the start of each row automatically
Each row is a separate block that the pointer jumps between
Pointer arithmetic on 2D arrays moves one row per increment
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic can step through any contiguous chunk of memory. A statically declared 2D array is one such chunk, laid out row after row.

questions.q: For which 2D array layouts can you set a pointer once to the first element and then reach every element just by incrementing it?
choices: A statically declared array such as int m[10][20]
A dynamically allocated array made with one malloc of rows * columns elements
An array of arrays where each row comes from its own separate malloc call
questions.explain: Both the static array and the single-malloc array keep every row in contiguous memory. With one malloc per row, only the elements within each row are contiguous.

questions.q: True or false: When a 2D array is built as an array of arrays (one malloc per row), a pointer used to walk the elements must be reset to the start of each row.
questions.explain: Each row is its own allocation, so the rows are not guaranteed to sit next to each other. Only the elements inside a row are contiguous.

questions.q: True or false: Pointer arithmetic only works on statically declared arrays, not on dynamically allocated ones.
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic works on dynamically allocated arrays too. With dynamic 2D arrays, what matters is whether the memory is contiguous.
